title: How to create a bibliography in Word on Mac: steps for Microsoft 365 and 2024

description: How to create a bibliography in Word on Mac: add sources on the References tab, insert citations, then build and update the list.

intro: To create a bibliography in Word on Mac, add each source with References > Insert Citation > Add new source, then place the list with References > Bibliography. Word builds the list from your citations, so you refresh it with Update Citations and Bibliography whenever you add or change a source.
tldr: Work in the Word desktop app. Word for the web can keep a list but cannot create citations or a bibliography.
Set your citation style first under References > Style, so every citation follows one format.
Add each source through References > Insert Citation > Add new source, then pick a Type of Source.
Place the list where it belongs with References > Bibliography, then choose the heading your guide uses.
After any change, click the list and choose Update Citations and Bibliography.

blocks.text: What Word builds for you

A bibliography in Word is not a typed list. It is a field that Word fills from the sources you save. When you add a source, Word keeps its details on your Mac, so you can cite it again later. The list updates from those saved details. If you type inside the list, the next update can replace your typing.

Two parts make this work. The citation is the short tag in your text, such as an author name and a page. The bibliography is the full list at the end. Both point at the same saved source, so a fix to the source fixes every place it appears.
Choose a citation style before you add sources

Set the style first. Go to References > Style and pick the format your course, journal, or employer asks for. Word applies that style to every citation and to the list. Changing it later works, but it means more updating and more chances for odd punctuation.

Check the style list in your own copy. A Microsoft Q&A thread on Word for Mac reported only MLA Seventh Edition in the list, while MLA now uses its Ninth Edition. The thread does not say whether a later update changed that. If your required edition is missing, ask your instructor or editor which format they accept.
Pick the right Type of Source

The Create Source dialog asks for a Type of Source first. Choose the type that matches the item, not the closest type. A journal article, a book, and a web page each need different fields. The style uses those fields to build each entry, so a wrong type leaves fields out or puts them in the wrong place.

Tick Show all bibliography fields if you want every box visible. Digital Trends describes that checkbox in its Word guide. Fill in author names in the order your style expects. Leave a box blank rather than typing a guess, because a guess prints in the list.
A worked example: citing one journal article

Say you cite an article by Jordan Lee from a journal. Click after the sentence that uses the article's idea. Choose References > Insert Citation > Add new source. Set the Type of Source to journal article, then enter the author, title, journal name, and page range. Click OK.

Word puts a citation tag at the cursor and saves the source. Later, when you cite Lee again, click where the tag belongs and choose References > Insert Citation. Pick the saved source from the list. You do not retype the details, so the spelling stays the same every time.
Placement matters too. Some styles put the citation before the full stop, and others put it after. Check your style guide for placement before you insert the tag.
Keep the list in sync after edits

The list updates only when you tell it to. After you add a source, click anywhere in the bibliography and choose Update Citations and Bibliography. Microsoft's training page gives the same tip. Repeat this before you save a final copy and after you change the style.

To change a source, edit the source itself. Point at a citation in the Citations pane, open its arrow, and choose Edit Source. For many changes at once, open Manage Sources. A publisher name that appears in many entries is a good case for a bulk edit.
Mistakes people make with a Word bibliography

items: Typing the list by hand. The next update can replace the typing, and your sources and list drift apart.
Starting the list in Word for the web. The web version keeps an existing list but cannot create one.
Changing the style, then forgetting to update. Some entries keep the old format until you update.
Adding sources after the final update. Refresh the list again before you save or send the file.
Mixing a reference manager add-in with Word's own list. Pick one system for each project.
Assuming the References tab is gone. It is often hidden in the ribbon settings, and one check shows it again.

blocks.text: When the list will not update

Sometimes the update spins and never finishes. One Microsoft Q&A user had about 1,000 ISO 690 citations in a roughly 500-page book, and the wait icon on Word for Mac did not clear. A moderator reported that splitting the document into smaller files fixed the problem in testing. That is a single report, not an official fix.
Test any split on a copy first. Keep the original file, and check page numbers, headings, and the list after you rebuild it. Smaller files are easier to update, but you then manage several files.
Bibliography or Works Cited

The same menu offers Bibliography and Works Cited. Both build a list from your saved sources. Pick the heading your style guide uses, because the heading is part of the format. You insert either one in the same place and in the same way.
Reference manager add-ins

Many people use a reference manager that connects to Word through an add-in. Guides disagree about where that add-in tab appears on a Mac. Some put it under References, and others put it under Add-Ins. Follow the install instructions from the add-in maker, and check their pricing page if cost matters to you.
Do not run two systems on one paper. If the add-in and Word's list both insert citations, the entries can conflict. Choose one system, and keep it for the whole document.
Check the finished list before you submit

Read the list once after the final update. Confirm that every cited source appears in the list, and that every entry has a matching citation in the text. Check italics, capital letters, and the order of author names against your style guide.
Word formats what you give it. It cannot fix a wrong author name or a date you typed incorrectly. Correct the source, then update again.
Which Word version you need

Microsoft's release notes list Word for Mac version 16.114.3, build 26102720, dated October 27, 2026. The two releases before it are described as quality and performance improvements only. None of the listed releases mention References or citation changes. Check your own version with Word > About Microsoft Word.
Keyboard shortcuts near citation work

Microsoft's shortcut lists show no Mac shortcut for Insert Citation or Bibliography. Use the ribbon for those. Footnotes and endnotes sit beside citations in many papers, so their shortcuts still help. ⌘⌥F inserts a footnote, and ⌘⌥E inserts an endnote.

⌘F9 inserts an empty field, which helps when you build a custom list. F9 updates the selected fields, but Microsoft notes it may conflict with a macOS shortcut. If F9 does nothing on your Mac, use the right-click menu on the list instead.
Next steps after your first bibliography

Once the list works, the next job is usually the citations in the body text. Read [how to insert a citation in Word on Mac](/how-to/insert-a-citation-in-word) for placement and style details. If the paper also needs a contents page, read [how to insert a table of contents in Word on Mac](/how-to/insert-a-table-of-contents-in-word).

faq.question: Can I create a bibliography in Word for the web?
faq.answer: No. Word for the web can keep an existing bibliography, but it cannot create citations or a new list. Open the file in the Word desktop app on your Mac to build one.

faq.question: Why is the References tab missing in Word on Mac?
faq.answer: It is probably hidden in the ribbon settings. Open Word > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar, select Popular Commands, and check References in the right column. A Microsoft Q&A answer reports this fixed the problem.

faq.question: How do I change the citation style after I added sources?
faq.answer: Open References > Style and pick the new style. Then click in the bibliography and choose Update Citations and Bibliography. Read the list afterward, because punctuation and italics can need a closer look.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for Insert Citation?
faq.answer: Microsoft's Mac shortcut lists do not show one for Insert Citation or Bibliography. Use the References tab for both. Footnotes have shortcuts, so ⌘⌥F is the one to learn first.

faq.question: Why does my bibliography keep showing an old entry?
faq.answer: The list has not updated yet. Right-click it, choose Update Field, then Update Entire Table. If you typed inside the list, the update can replace that typing, so edit the source instead.

faq.question: Does Word for Mac include MLA 9th edition?
faq.answer: The evidence is unclear. One Microsoft Q&A community answer says only MLA Seventh Edition appeared on Word for Mac, and the thread does not say whether an update fixed it. Check your version and the style list before you rely on it.

task: Create a bibliography in Word on Mac
appliesTo: Word for Microsoft 365 and Word 2024 on macOS
requirements: Word for Microsoft 365 or Word 2024 on a Mac
Source details: author, title, and publication information
The Word desktop app, not Word for the web

steps.name: Open the References tab
steps.text: Open your document in the Word desktop app. Click the References tab in the ribbon. If it is missing, open Word > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar, select Popular Commands, and check References in the right column.
steps.tip: Microsoft's Mac menu labels vary a little by version. Match the ribbon names you see on your screen.

steps.name: Choose a citation style
steps.text: Click References, then Style. Pick the style your instructor, journal, or employer requires. Word applies it to every citation and to the list in this file.
steps.tip: Set the style before you add sources, so you do not need a full update later.

steps.name: Place the cursor after the cited text
steps.text: Click right after the words or sentence you are citing. Check your style guide for citation placement, because some styles put the tag before the full stop and others after it.

steps.name: Add a new source
steps.text: Click References, then Insert Citation, and choose Add new source. The Create Source dialog opens.

steps.name: Fill in the Create Source dialog
steps.text: Pick a Type of Source, such as Journal Article. Enter the author, title, and publication details. Tick Show all bibliography fields to see every box. Click OK. Word inserts the citation and saves the source for reuse.
steps.tip: Leave a box blank rather than guessing. A wrong detail prints in the list.

steps.name: Cite a saved source again
steps.text: Put the cursor where the new citation belongs, then choose References > Insert Citation. Pick the source from the list. The citation uses the same saved details every time.

steps.name: Place the bibliography
steps.text: Put the cursor on the page where the list should appear, usually at the end of the document. Click the arrow next to Bibliography on the References tab, then select Bibliography or Works Cited.

steps.name: Update the list after changes
steps.text: Click anywhere inside the list. Choose References > Update Citations and Bibliography. Repeat this after you add, delete, or edit a source, or after you change the style.
steps.tip: Microsoft's training page gives this tip. Run it again before you save a final copy.

steps.name: Edit a source later
steps.text: Point at a citation in the Citations pane, open its arrow, and choose Edit Source. For many changes at once, open Manage Sources and edit the saved sources. Then update the list.
steps.tip: Edit the source, not the typed text in the list. Word can overwrite typed changes.

steps.name: Check the list before you submit
steps.text: Read every entry against your style guide. Confirm that each cited source appears in the list, and that each entry has a matching citation in the text. Check italics, capital letters, and author order.
steps.tip: If an entry looks wrong, fix the source details, then update the list again.

troubleshooting.problem: The References tab is missing from the ribbon
troubleshooting.fix: Open Word > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar. Confirm Popular Commands is selected, then check the References box in the right column. The tab normally sits sixth from the left.

troubleshooting.problem: The bibliography does not update or still shows old text
troubleshooting.fix: Right-click the list, choose Update Field, then choose Update Entire Table. This is an accepted Microsoft Q&A answer. Afterward, check the source details you edited.

troubleshooting.problem: The update spins and never finishes on a long book
troubleshooting.fix: A Microsoft Q&A moderator reported that splitting the document into smaller files fixed it in testing. Work on a copy first, and check page numbers and headings after the split.

troubleshooting.problem: APA 6th Edition repeats the title for works by the same author
troubleshooting.fix: Edit the citation and tick the Title checkbox. Microsoft's APA, MLA, Chicago page describes this fix.

troubleshooting.problem: Word for the web will not create a bibliography
troubleshooting.fix: Word for the web cannot create citations or a bibliography. Open the file in the Word desktop app on your Mac, then insert the list there.

troubleshooting.problem: The MLA edition you need is not in the style list
troubleshooting.fix: A Microsoft Q&A community answer reports only MLA Seventh Edition on Word for Mac. Check your version, then ask your instructor which format they accept.
